title: When a Measurement Is From the Past: Stamps, a History of the State, Correcting the State as It Was and Carrying the Correction Forward, and Finding the Delay Between Two Clocks

questions.question: What time should a measurement be stamped with?
options: The time the filter used it
The time of the last odometry step
Any time, as long as it is consistent
questions.explanation: The measurement describes the world at the moment it was taken. Arrival is that plus a delay which has to be known.

questions.question: A late fix taken for the present left a steady error of:
options: Nothing: a late fix is still a fix
questions.explanation: At about 2 m/s a fix 0.25 s old is half a metre behind. Treating it as the position now pulls the estimate back by that much, every second.

questions.question: Comparing the fix with the state of its own time gave an rms error of:
questions.explanation: Both ways of allowing for the delay were within the 3 cm noise of the fix, and ten times better than ignoring it.

questions.question: The lag between the gyro and the wheels was found as:
questions.explanation: The gyro and the wheels see the same turning. Sliding one against the other and keeping the shift with the largest correlation gave the true 0.12 s.

questions.question: When does extrapolating by the velocity fail?
options: When the velocity changes during the delay, as when the robot brakes to a stop
When the fix is noisier than the odometry
When the delay is under a tenth of a second
questions.explanation: Extrapolating assumes the velocity held over the delay. A robot that braked to a stop in that time was put 0.25 m further on than it was.

questions.question: What does the history method need that the others do not?
options: The velocity at the time of arrival
A memory of the states long enough to reach back past the delay
questions.explanation: To compare a fix with the state at its stamp, the estimator must still have that state. The history here holds 4000 of them.
